title: Serving without burning out
hookLine: the acrobat's balance: care for yourself too (SN 47.19)
tomorrow: Mai's been asked to teach little kids. what can a walk teach first?

cards: Running on empty can start to feel like proof you care: the late night, the yes to every ask, the quick "i'm fine" text. Mai has had that week. The mural on art day.
Water and company for Jess through the fever. Ten minutes at the creek that turned into an afternoon. And last night, art cards for the county jail until almost two.
This morning she fell asleep in studio with a brush in her hand, and she hasn't sat on her own once all week.
The suttas answer her with a balancing act: two acrobats, one bamboo pole, and an argument about who keeps whom from falling.

teach.b: The Buddha tells it near a town called Sedaka. An acrobat sets up his bamboo pole and calls his apprentice to climb up and stand on his shoulders. Then he lays out the plan.
You look after me, and I'll look after you.
Guarded by each other, we'll show our skill, earn our fee, and come down safe. The apprentice says no. Teacher, you look after yourself, and I'll look after myself.
Each of us guarded by our own care, we'll show our skill and come down safe. And the Buddha says the apprentice has it right. Guarding yourself, you guard others.
Guarding others, you guard yourself. Then he names both halves.
You guard yourself by sati, mindfulness, practiced, developed and made much of. You guard others by patience, by not harming, by loving-kindness, metta, and by sympathy.
That's the teaching, and the story is kept among the Buddha's sayings on mindfulness. In this sutta, keeping your own practice isn't time taken away from caring. It's the footing the care stands on.
A teacher who loses his balance drops the one on his shoulders.
Run the week back through that. A question asked on a street. A lamp of your own.
A sick monk washed. A tree left standing. A road toward the man everyone fled.
Every one of those needed someone standing steady. For Mai, the jail cards are real care. So is the sit she skipped.

how: Some Buddhist teachers who train chaplains and volunteers ask them to keep a daily sit alongside their service, and the acrobat story from the Samyutta Nikaya is one they tell.

games.q: what does “serving without burning out” mean?
o: keeping your own footing so you can keep helping
stepping back from helping until you feel ready
putting others first until there's nothing left

games.q: two acrobats, one pole — tap the pairs.
p: each one watches their own footing

s: in Buddhism, tending your own practice while others need you is selfish
the Buddha sided with the apprentice: guarding yourself, you guard others.
in the sutta, you guard others by patience, not harming, loving-kindness and sympathy
and guarding others that way guards you too.
the story tells helpers to stop serving until they feel fully rested
both acrobats still climb and perform; each minds their own footing while they work.

games.q: at art day, a kid paints right over the corner you spent an hour on, and your jaw tightens. by the acrobat sutta, what guards you here?
o: patience and no harm toward him; guarding him that way guards you
walking off to protect your peace; guarding yourself comes first
fixing it fast and saying nothing; the mural matters more than you
games.why: the Buddha says guarding others, by patience, harmlessness, kindness and sympathy, is also how you guard yourself. the patient answer keeps your own mind steady.

practice: Set down whatever you're holding: the phone, the pen, the brush. Choose one sound near you, a fan, traffic, your own breath, and let your attention rest on it, the way an acrobat's weight settles on one steady foot.
When the mind runs to the list of what's still owed, come back to the sound.

wordCard.voice: Serving without burning out: keeping your own footing so the care can go on. The acrobat's apprentice minded their own footing, and so kept both of them up.

orig.note: Pali: mindfulness; in the acrobat sutta, the way you guard yourself.

carryVoice: Carry this: balance. Keep your own footing, and the one on your shoulders stays up. A week of serving, done.
